name: hf-gradebook
description: Two parallel tracks build a gradebook: statistics helpers, and CSV report plus command line using them.
goal: Build a small Python package `gradebook` (standard library only) that turns a class's scores, given as CSV text with a name column and a score column, into a ranked plain-text table with letter grades and a class summary line, plus a command line front end. The directory `gradebook/` and its `__init__.py` already exist, and `tests/test_gradebook.py` already exists and must not be edited. Two tracks run at the same time and cannot talk to each other: `stats` writes `gradebook/stats.py`; `report` writes `gradebook/report.py` and `gradebook/cli.py`. The shared interface is `stats.letter_grade(score)` and `stats.summarize(values)`, described identically in both track prompts. At the end the test suite in `tests/` must pass.

tracks.name: stats
tracks.prompt:
Write the file `gradebook/stats.py` (Python 3, standard library only). The package `gradebook` already exists with an `__init__.py`. Write only this one file and do not edit anything else, including `tests/`. Another builder is writing `gradebook/report.py` and `gradebook/cli.py` at the same time; they will call `stats.letter_grade(score)` and `stats.summarize(values)` exactly as described below, so keep those names, arguments and return shapes.

Provide exactly these functions:
- `mean(values)` -> float: the arithmetic mean of a non-empty sequence of numbers. Raise `ValueError` if it is empty.
- `median(values)` -> float: the middle value of the numbers in sorted order; for an even count, the mean of the two middle values. Raise `ValueError` if empty. It must not modify the sequence passed in.
- `letter_grade(score)` -> str: `"A"` when score >= 90, `"B"` when >= 80, `"C"` when >= 70, `"D"` when >= 60, otherwise `"F"`. Scores are floats, so 89.99 is `"B"`, 90.0 is `"A"` and 104.5 is `"A"`.
- `summarize(values)` -> dict with exactly the keys `count` (int), `mean`, `median`, `min`, `max` for a sequence of numbers. For an empty sequence do not raise: return `{"count": 0, "mean": None, "median": None, "min": None, "max": None}`.

tracks.name: report
tracks.prompt:
Write the files `gradebook/report.py` and `gradebook/cli.py` (Python 3, standard library only). The package `gradebook` already exists with an `__init__.py`. Write only these two files and do not edit anything else, including `tests/`. Another builder is writing `gradebook/stats.py` at the same time; do not write that file. Import it with `from gradebook import stats` and use only these two functions from it, which will behave as follows:
- `stats.letter_grade(score)` -> str: `"A"` for score >= 90, `"B"` for >= 80, `"C"` for >= 70, `"D"` for >= 60, otherwise `"F"`.
- `stats.summarize(values)` -> dict with the keys `count` (int), `mean`, `median`, `min`, `max` for a list of numbers (for an empty list the count is 0 and the others are `None`; you will not need that case).

`gradebook/report.py` provides:
- `parse_rows(text)` -> list of `(name, score)` tuples with `name` a str and `score` a float. `text` is CSV with two columns, name and score; read it with the `csv` module. Ignore lines that are empty or contain only whitespace. The first remaining line is a header, and is skipped, when it has at least two fields and its second field (stripped) is not a number that `float()` accepts, for example `name,score`; any other line is a data row. Every data row must have exactly two fields, a non-empty name once stripped, and a stripped score that `float()` accepts; otherwise raise `ValueError`. Names are returned stripped. Rows keep their input order. A header line is only recognised as the first remaining line, so a later line with a non-numeric score is an error.
- `render(rows)` -> str. If `rows` is empty return exactly `No scores`. Otherwise return these lines joined with `"\n"` and no trailing newline: first `Name | Score | Grade`; then one line per row, ordered by score from highest to lowest and, for equal scores, by name in plain string order (case-sensitive, so `Zed` comes before `bob`), each formatted `{name} | {score:.1f} | {grade}` where grade is `stats.letter_grade(score)` applied to the unrounded score (so a score of 89.96 is printed as `90.0` but still gets `B`); then a last line `Class: {count} students, mean {mean:.1f}, median {median:.1f}` with the numbers taken from `stats.summarize` of all the scores, using `1 student` instead of `1 students` when the count is 1.

`gradebook/cli.py` provides:
- `main(argv=None, stdin=None, stdout=None, stderr=None)` -> int. When an argument is None use `sys.argv[1:]`, `sys.stdin`, `sys.stdout` and `sys.stderr`, looked up when `main` runs and not at import time. With more than one item in `argv`, write `usage: python -m gradebook.cli [file.csv]` and a newline to stderr and return 2. With one item, it is the path of a CSV file: read it as UTF-8 (open it with `newline=""`). With none, read all of `stdin`. Then write `report.render(report.parse_rows(text))` followed by a newline to stdout and return 0. If reading the file raises `OSError` or parsing raises `ValueError`, write `error: <message>` and a newline to stderr, write nothing to stdout, and return 2.
- End the file with `if __name__ == "__main__": raise SystemExit(main())`.

expected_outcome: gradebook/stats.py, gradebook/report.py and gradebook/cli.py exist and agree on the shared stats interface, and the gates pass: the tests pass and all three modules import.
